posts.title: AI Pair Programming and Vibe Coding: Benefits and Risks for Businesses
posts.description: AI coding assistants and vibe coding: where they help, where they fail, security, quality, IP and privacy risks, and how businesses can use them safely.
posts.keywords: vibe coding risks, ai pair programming, can ai build a whole app, is ai generated code secure, ai coding assistants for business, do i still need developers, ai generated code quality
posts.intro: Software development has changed more in the past few years than in the previous decade. AI assistants can now write functions, explain unfamiliar code, generate tests and, in the hands of enthusiasts, produce entire working prototypes from a conversation. The term “vibe coding” has stuck to the most extreme version of this: describing what you want in natural language and accepting whatever the AI produces, without examining the code. For businesses, the promise is intoxicating: cheaper, faster software, perhaps without needing developers at all. The reality is more nuanced. AI is a powerful accelerator for skilled people and a risky shortcut for unskilled ones. This guide separates the genuine benefits from the hype, explains the real risks around security, quality, maintenance, intellectual property and privacy, and gives practical guidance for using AI in software work responsibly, whether you build in-house, hire a team or experiment yourself.
takeaways: AI coding tools speed up routine coding, prototyping, testing and documentation, especially for experienced developers who can review the output.
Vibe coding, accepting generated code without understanding it, is fine for throwaway prototypes and risky for anything customers or data depend on.
AI-generated code can contain security flaws, bugs, outdated patterns and subtle errors, and can accumulate technical debt quickly.
You still need engineering judgement: architecture, requirements, testing, security review and maintenance do not disappear.
Set policies on tools, confidential code and data, require review and testing, and ask vendors how they use AI.

blocks.text: What these terms mean

**AI pair programming** means a developer works alongside an AI assistant integrated in their editor or terminal. The assistant suggests code, completes functions, explains errors, drafts tests and refactors, while the human directs, reviews and decides. **Agentic coding tools** go further, carrying out multi-step tasks such as editing several files, running tests and fixing failures, still ideally under human supervision. **Vibe coding** is the informal term for building software by prompting an AI and accepting the results with little or no review of the code itself, judging by whether the app seems to work. The terms describe a spectrum from careful, expert use to hands-off experimentation.

blocks.title: The spectrum of AI-assisted development
rows: Writes code; accepts or rejects suggestions
Asks questions, reviews and integrates answers
Directs tasks and reviews diffs and tests
Describes outcomes; accepts output with little review
High for anything beyond throwaway use

blocks.text: Where AI coding tools genuinely help

items: **Boilerplate and repetitive code:** forms, data models, API clients, configuration and glue code.

**Prototyping:** getting a working demo in hours to test an idea or show stakeholders, complementing no-code approaches; see [no-code vs. low-code vs. custom code](/blog/no-code-vs-low-code-vs-custom-code).
**Learning and exploration:** explaining unfamiliar code, languages and libraries, and suggesting approaches.
**Tests and documentation:** drafting unit tests, comments and README files, which developers can refine.
**Refactoring and migrations:** mechanical changes across files, with tests to verify.
**Debugging:** interpreting error messages and suggesting fixes.
**Lowering barriers:** domain experts and small businesses can build simple internal tools they could not before.

blocks.text: Studies and developer surveys report meaningful productivity gains on many tasks, particularly for routine work and for experienced developers, though results vary by task, tool and skill, and some measurements show that review and correction time can offset gains. Treat claims of enormous multipliers sceptically and measure results in your own context.
The real risks
1. Security vulnerabilities

AI models learn from vast amounts of code, including insecure examples, and may generate code with common flaws: injection vulnerabilities, weak authentication, insecure defaults, exposed secrets, missing authorisation checks and unsafe handling of user input. They may also suggest outdated or non-existent packages, creating supply-chain risks, as attackers can register package names that models tend to hallucinate. Code that appears to work can be dangerously insecure. The practices in our [mobile app security checklist](/blog/mobile-app-security-checklist) still apply and must be actively checked rather than assumed.
2. Quality, correctness and hidden bugs

Generated code can pass a casual test and still fail on edge cases, mishandle errors, perform badly at scale or implement the wrong logic confidently. Without understanding, you cannot spot these problems. Business rules, such as pricing, tax and permissions, are particularly risky to leave to an unreviewed model.
3. Technical debt and maintainability

AI makes it fast to add code, and just as fast to add duplicated, inconsistent and poorly structured code. Without architectural discipline, projects become tangled quickly, and the person who must maintain them later may find a codebase nobody understands, including the person who prompted it. See technical debt explained for how this cost builds up.
4. Intellectual property and licensing

Questions remain about copyright and licensing of AI-generated code, including whether outputs may resemble licensed training material and who owns the result. Vendor terms differ on indemnification, and the legal position is evolving and varies by jurisdiction. If you build products for sale or sensitive work, take legal advice and review tool terms, and ensure your contracts address AI use, as discussed in the [software development contract guide](/blog/software-development-contract-guide).
5. Privacy and confidentiality

Pasting proprietary code, credentials or customer data into an AI tool sends it to a third party, and, depending on settings and plan, it may be retained or used to improve models. Developers using personal accounts on consumer tools can leak confidential material without realising it. Apply the questions from [AI privacy and security for small business](/blog/ai-privacy-and-security-for-small-business) to coding tools too.
6. Over-reliance and skill erosion

If juniors lean on AI before learning fundamentals, they may never develop the judgement to evaluate it. Teams can lose understanding of their own systems. Debugging code you did not write and do not understand is hard.
7. The last-mile problem

Getting to “80 percent working” is now fast. The remaining 20 percent, security, performance, reliability, accessibility, integrations, edge cases and deployment, is where real software engineering lives, and it is exactly what vibe-coded prototypes often lack.

blocks.title: A working demo is not a production system
blocks.text: An app that looks fine in a demo may lack authentication, data protection, backups, monitoring and error handling. Treat generated prototypes as sketches, not as foundations for customer data or revenue.
Prototype vs. production

blocks.title: Where vibe coding is acceptable, and where it is not

left.title: Reasonable uses
points: Throwaway prototypes and demos
Personal or internal one-off scripts with no sensitive data
Exploring ideas before specifying requirements
Learning and experimentation

right.title: Dangerous uses
points: Handling customer data, payments or health information
Customer-facing products without expert review
Core business logic nobody understands
Systems that must be maintained for years

blocks.text: Do you still need developers?

Yes, but their work shifts. Developers who use AI well spend less time on typing and more on defining requirements, designing architecture, reviewing and testing code, integrating systems, securing and operating software and making trade-offs the AI cannot judge. Non-developers can now build more themselves, which changes who builds what, but responsibility for correctness, security and maintenance remains. Businesses should expect AI to make good teams faster and clients’ expectations higher, not to eliminate the need for engineering discipline. If you are hiring or evaluating teams, see [how to choose a software development company](/blog/how-to-choose-a-software-development-company) and ask how they use AI.
How to use AI coding tools safely

blocks.title: Practical guardrails
items: Choose approved tools with business plans that offer data controls and clear terms, not personal accounts
Never put secrets, credentials or customer data into prompts or code sent to external tools
Require human review of all AI-generated code, as for any contribution
Run automated tests, linters, static analysis and dependency vulnerability scans in your pipeline; see [DevOps for small teams](/blog/devops-and-ci-cd-for-small-teams)
Verify that suggested packages exist, are maintained and are trusted before installing
Have developers write or review tests for important logic, and use AI to help generate more, not to replace judgement
Do security reviews and, for sensitive systems, independent penetration testing
Keep architecture and coding standards explicit so generated code follows them
Document decisions and keep humans who understand the system accountable
Track outcomes: defects, review time and delivery speed, not just lines produced

items.title: Define the task and constraints
items.text: Clear requirements, standards and acceptance criteria.

items.title: Generate in small steps
items.text: Ask for small, reviewable changes, not entire applications at once.

items.title: Review and understand
items.text: Read the code; ask the AI to explain unclear parts and challenge it.

items.title: Test thoroughly
items.text: Automated tests plus manual checks of edge cases and failure modes.

items.title: Scan and verify
items.text: Security and dependency checks.

items.title: Merge through normal review
items.text: Pull requests and approvals as with any code.

blocks.text: What business owners should do

items: **Ask your developers and vendors how they use AI,** what safeguards they have and how it affects pricing and quality.
**Write a short policy:** approved tools, forbidden data, review requirements and ownership.
**Be sceptical of “AI built it in a weekend” claims** for production systems.
**Use AI to prototype and learn,** then involve experienced engineers to harden and own what matters.
**Include AI-related terms in contracts:** IP, confidentiality, security and disclosure.
**Invest in maintainability:** documentation, tests and clear structure keep AI-assisted code manageable.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Shipping vibe-coded software with real customer data.**
**Pasting secrets and proprietary code into consumer tools.**
**Skipping tests and review** because the output “looks right”.
**Letting AI generate sprawling, inconsistent code** with no architecture.
**Assuming AI removes the need for security expertise.**
**Ignoring licensing and IP questions.**
**Treating productivity claims as certain.**

blocks.text: Want the speed of AI-assisted development with the discipline of professional engineering? We use modern tools responsibly, with review, testing and security built into every project.
blocks.label: Build software the right way

faqs.question: Can AI build a whole app?
faqs.answer: AI can generate working prototypes and substantial parts of applications, but production software also needs architecture, security, testing, integration, deployment and maintenance, which require human engineering judgement.

faqs.question: Is AI-generated code secure?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. It can include common vulnerabilities, insecure defaults or unsafe dependencies. Review it, test it, scan it and apply secure coding practices like any other code.

faqs.question: Do I still need developers?
faqs.answer: Yes. AI changes how developers work and lets non-developers build simple tools, but responsibility for requirements, architecture, quality, security and maintenance remains with skilled people.

faqs.question: What is vibe coding?
faqs.answer: Vibe coding means building software by describing what you want to an AI and accepting its output with little or no review of the code. It suits throwaway prototypes but is risky for anything that handles real data or must be maintained.

faqs.question: Is it safe to paste my code into AI tools?
faqs.answer: Only with approved tools whose data handling you have reviewed. Avoid sharing secrets, customer data and confidential code with unvetted or consumer tools, and check retention and training policies.

posts.title: No-Code vs. Low-Code vs. Custom Code: How to Choose
posts.shortTitle: No-code vs. low-code vs. custom code
posts.description: No-code vs low-code vs custom code: speed, cost, flexibility, scalability, security and lock-in, with a decision guide and when to move to code.
posts.keywords: no code vs low code vs custom code, can i build an app with no code, limits of no code, when to switch from no code to custom code, no code platform risks, low code development, build vs buy software
posts.intro: A decade ago, building software meant hiring developers. Today, anyone can drag and drop their way to a working app, website or workflow using no-code and low-code platforms, and the results can be genuinely impressive. That has changed the economics of building products, especially for founders and small teams testing ideas. But the new options also create confusion. Is no-code a serious foundation for a business, or a toy? What is the difference from low-code? When does custom code become the better choice? The honest answer is that each approach has a sweet spot and predictable limits. This guide explains the three approaches, compares them on speed, cost, flexibility, scalability, security and ownership, shows which kinds of projects suit each and offers a decision framework, including how to start with no-code and move on without a painful rewrite.
takeaways: No-code uses visual tools for non-developers; low-code adds scripting for developers and technical users; custom code gives full control.
No-code and low-code are excellent for validation, internal tools and simple products, delivering speed and low initial cost.
Limits appear in performance, complex logic, integrations, data ownership, customisation and per-user pricing as you scale.
Custom code costs more upfront but offers flexibility, ownership and long-term economics for core products.
A staged approach, validating with no-code and rebuilding the proven core in code, often gives the best of both.

blocks.text: Three approaches defined

**No-code** platforms let people build applications through visual interfaces, templates and configuration, with no programming required. Examples of categories include website builders, app builders, database and form tools, and workflow automators. **Low-code** platforms provide visual development plus the ability to write code for custom logic and integrations, aiming to speed up professional developers and empower technical “citizen developers”. **Custom code** means writing software in a programming language and framework, giving complete control over behaviour, architecture and infrastructure.

blocks.title: The spectrum at a glance
rows: Limited to what the platform exposes
Prototypes, internal tools, simple apps and sites
Core products, complex logic and scale

blocks.text: What no-code does brilliantly

items: **Speed:** a working prototype in days, which makes testing ideas cheap.
**Low initial cost:** subscriptions replace large development budgets.
**Empowering the people who understand the problem:** operations, marketing and founders can build and iterate without waiting for engineering.
**Good fit for standard patterns:** forms, databases, dashboards, directories, simple marketplaces, membership sites and workflow automation.
**Easy changes:** edit and republish without a development cycle.

blocks.text: This makes no-code a natural tool for the validation stage described in the [MVP development guide](/blog/mvp-development-guide-for-startups): learn whether anyone wants the product before investing in engineering. Workflow tools discussed in [Zapier alternatives](/blog/zapier-alternatives) are a related category.
Where no-code and low-code struggle

blocks.title: The limits are predictable
blocks.text: Most no-code and low-code projects hit similar walls: unusual logic, performance at scale, complex integrations, fine-grained permissions and cost growth. Knowing them in advance helps you plan an exit rather than being trapped.

items: **Customisation limits:** the platform decides what is possible; a feature outside its model may be impossible or require awkward workarounds.
**Performance and scale:** large datasets, complex queries and high traffic can strain visual platforms and may hit hard limits.
**Pricing growth:** per-user, per-record or per-run charges can climb steeply as the product succeeds.
**Vendor lock-in:** your app lives on the platform; exporting logic, not just data, may be impossible, so migration means a rebuild.
**Data ownership and control:** where data lives, how it is backed up and who can access it are determined by the vendor.
**Security and compliance:** you inherit the platform’s security model and certifications, which may not meet regulatory needs.
**Maintainability:** complex visual logic can become tangled and hard to document, test and version.
**Platform risk:** pricing, features and even the company’s existence can change.

blocks.text: Low-code: the middle ground

Low-code platforms offer more power than no-code: custom scripts, API integrations, richer data models and sometimes the ability to deploy to your own infrastructure. They suit internal business applications, workflows and portals where a professional developer can combine visual building with code. The trade-offs are a steeper learning curve, a platform-specific skill set and, again, some lock-in. They can be a strong choice for enterprise internal tools and process apps, less so for consumer products that need distinctive experiences and total control.
Where custom code wins

items: **Unique products and competitive advantage:** when the software is the business, you need to control it fully.
**Complex logic and integrations:** deep business rules, unusual data flows and bespoke connections to other systems; see [what API integration is](/blog/what-is-api-integration).
**Performance and scale:** tailored architecture, caching and infrastructure.
**Security and compliance:** control over data location, access, audit trails and testing.
**Ownership and portability:** you own the code and can host and move it as you wish.
**Long-term economics:** no per-user licence growth, which can be much cheaper at scale.
**Experience and brand:** complete freedom in design and behaviour.

blocks.text: Side-by-side comparison

blocks.title: No-code vs. low-code vs. custom code
rows: Subscription that can grow with usage
Hosting and maintenance; no per-user licences
Depends on vendor plus your code

blocks.text: How to decide

items.title: Clarify the goal
items.text: Is this a test, an internal tool or your core product?

items.title: List must-have requirements
items.text: Logic, integrations, performance, security and compliance needs.

items.title: Check platform fit
items.text: Can a no-code or low-code tool meet them without hacks? Build a quick proof of the hardest part.

items.title: Estimate three-year cost
items.text: Include subscriptions at expected volume, add-ons and maintenance versus building and running custom.

items.title: Assess lock-in and exit
items.text: What happens if you outgrow or lose the platform?

items.title: Choose a staged path if unsure
items.text: Start light, validate and plan the transition.

blocks.title: Matching project to approach
rows: No-code site builder, or a lightweight custom build; see [how much a business website costs](/blog/how-much-does-a-business-website-cost)
Idea validation or MVP with simple logic
Internal tracking, approvals and reporting tools
Low-code or no-code, if data sensitivity allows
Workflow tools, custom code for critical flows
Customer-facing SaaS or marketplace at scale
Custom code, possibly after a no-code prototype
Custom or carefully vetted platforms with appropriate compliance
Mobile app with deep device features

blocks.text: Start light, move smart

A common and sensible strategy is to prototype in no-code, learn from real users and then rebuild the proven core in code when needs outgrow the platform. The no-code version becomes the specification, with real data on what users do, which saves time and money. To make the move easy, document logic and data models, keep data exportable, avoid platform-specific tricks where possible and design APIs and data structures cleanly. Moving gradually, one module at a time, reduces risk. This mirrors the staged thinking in [custom software vs. off-the-shelf](/blog/custom-software-vs-off-the-shelf).

blocks.title: Signs you are outgrowing no-code
items: You spend more time working around the platform than building features
Costs grow faster than revenue as usage increases
Performance problems appear with real data volumes
Customers or regulators ask for security or compliance you cannot provide
You need integrations or logic the platform cannot support
The product has become your core business and lock-in feels dangerous
You cannot test, version or document the app to the standard you need

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Choosing the platform before the problem is clear.**
**Assuming no-code means no maintenance,** when someone must still own, test and update the app.
**Ignoring pricing at scale.**
**Building a core product on a platform without an exit plan.**
**Underestimating complexity** and ending up with unmaintainable visual spaghetti.
**Dismissing no-code entirely** and spending months building what a prototype could have tested.
**Forgetting security and privacy,** particularly with customer data.

blocks.text: If you are unsure which route fits, review [how to choose a tech stack](/blog/choose-a-tech-stack-for-your-startup) for the broader decision framework.
Not sure whether to build with no-code, low-code or custom code? We assess your goals and constraints, prototype quickly where it helps and build custom software when it is the right foundation.
blocks.label: Choose the right approach

faqs.question: Can I build an app with no code?
faqs.answer: Yes, for many simple apps, internal tools and prototypes. No-code platforms can produce working products quickly, though complex logic, scale, integrations and customisation can hit platform limits.

faqs.question: What are the limits of no-code?
faqs.answer: Limits include customisation, performance at scale, pricing that grows with usage, vendor lock-in, limited control over data and security and difficulty maintaining complex logic.

faqs.question: When should I switch from no-code to custom code?
faqs.answer: When you outgrow the platform’s capabilities, costs escalate, performance suffers, compliance demands increase or the product becomes core to your business and lock-in is too risky.

faqs.question: What is the difference between no-code and low-code?
faqs.answer: No-code requires no programming and uses visual configuration, while low-code adds the ability to write custom code for logic and integrations, aimed at developers and technical users.

faqs.question: Is no-code cheaper than custom development?
faqs.answer: Usually at the start, yes. Over time, subscription costs at scale and the need for workarounds can erode that advantage, so compare total cost over several years.

posts.title: Pricing Your Software Services: Hourly, Fixed or Retainer
posts.description: How to price software and web development services: hourly, fixed price, retainers and value-based pricing, how to calculate rates, scope and raise prices.
posts.keywords: pricing software services, hourly vs fixed price development, how to price a retainer, value based pricing agency, how to raise your rates, freelancer pricing guide, how to quote a web project
posts.intro: Whether you are a freelance developer, a small agency or an in-house team charging internal clients, pricing is one of the hardest parts of selling software services. Charge too little and you work for free; charge too much and prospects walk away. Choose the wrong model and you absorb all the risk of overruns, or you leave money on the table when you deliver faster than expected. Clients, meanwhile, struggle to compare quotes that are structured in completely different ways. This guide looks at the pricing problem from the provider’s side, while helping buyers understand what they are seeing. It explains the main models, hourly, fixed price, retainers and value-based pricing, how to calculate a sustainable rate, how to structure and communicate quotes, how to protect yourself from scope creep and how to raise prices confidently.
takeaways: No model is universally best: choose by how certain the scope is, how much value you create and how the client prefers to buy.
Calculate your costs and a sustainable target rate first, then adjust for market, expertise and demand.
Fixed prices need clear scope and change control; hourly rates need trust and transparency; retainers suit ongoing work.
Value-based pricing aligns fees with client outcomes but requires understanding their business.
Present options, explain assumptions and review prices regularly; underpricing harms quality and sustainability.

blocks.text: Why pricing is hard in software

Software work is uncertain, the value delivered varies enormously and clients often cannot judge quality or effort. The same feature may take one developer a day and another a week. A small tool might save a client millions, or nothing. Add the temptation to compete on price, and many providers drift into undervaluing their work. Understanding the models and the thinking behind each helps you choose deliberately. The buyer’s view, covered in [software project estimation](/blog/software-project-estimation), is the mirror image of this guide.
Start with your numbers

Before choosing a model, know the minimum you must earn. For a freelancer, work out your target annual income, add costs such as tax, insurance, equipment, software, training, marketing and unpaid time off, then divide by the billable hours you can realistically sell. Billable utilisation is far below total working hours because of sales, admin, learning and gaps between projects, often in the range of half to two-thirds of the week, depending on the business. For an agency, include salaries, overhead, management, sales and profit, and calculate a blended rate or per-person day rate.

blocks.title: Rate calculation inputs
rows: What the business or you need to earn after all costs
Tax, insurance, tools, hosting, premises, equipment, accounting and legal
Sales, admin, learning, meetings that are not charged, holidays and sickness
Hours you can reliably sell, not total working hours
Experience, specialisation, demand and what comparable providers charge
Fixed-price risk, slow-paying clients and scope uncertainty

blocks.title: Price to be sustainable, not just competitive
blocks.text: Underpricing leads to rushed work, burnout, poor communication and no budget for improvement. Clients who value quality accept fair prices; clients who only compare the lowest hourly rate are rarely your best customers.
Hourly and day rates (time and materials)
The client pays for the time spent, at an agreed rate, usually with periodic invoices and often an estimate or cap. It is simple and flexible.

items: **Advantages:** fair for uncertain or evolving scope, easy to start, reflects actual effort, and lets clients change direction.
**Disadvantages:** penalises efficiency (the faster you work, the less you earn), invites scrutiny of hours, gives clients no price certainty and caps your income by time.
**Best for:** discovery, consulting, maintenance, projects with uncertain requirements and agile work.
**Tips:** give estimates and ranges, report progress transparently, agree a cap or approval point for overruns and consider day rates for large chunks of work.

blocks.text: Fixed-price projects

The client pays an agreed price for a defined scope and deliverables, usually in milestones. It offers cost certainty for the buyer and rewards efficiency for the provider, but moves estimation risk to you.

items: **Advantages:** easy for clients to approve and compare, rewards speed and expertise, aligns with outcomes.
**Disadvantages:** scope creep and underestimation hurt you, discourages flexibility and can cause disputes over what is included.
**Best for:** well-defined projects, such as a brochure website, a standard integration or a clearly specified feature set.

**Tips:** run a paid discovery first, write a detailed scope with explicit exclusions, state assumptions, include a change process and contingency and tie payments to milestones. See [software development contract guide](/blog/software-development-contract-guide) for the clauses to include.

left.title: Hourly or time and materials
points: Flexible when requirements change
Client carries budget uncertainty; you carry reputation risk of delays
Income tied to time spent
Suits discovery and ongoing work

right.title: Fixed price
points: Certainty for the client
You carry estimation and scope risk
Efficiency increases your margin
Suits well-defined deliverables

blocks.text: Retainers

A retainer is a recurring monthly fee for a defined level of service: a block of hours, a set of deliverables or access to a team. It provides predictable revenue for you and priority access for the client. It is common for maintenance, support, ongoing development and advisory work.

items: **Define what is included:** hours, response times, types of work and what falls outside.
**Decide about unused hours:** whether they roll over, expire or are refunded.
**Set reporting and review rhythms** so the client sees value.
**Price for the commitment:** retainers often include a modest discount for the guaranteed income, balanced against availability commitments.
**Include notice periods** and a review of scope and price annually.

blocks.text: Examples include website care and maintenance, which we describe from the client’s perspective in [website maintenance plans and costs](/blog/website-maintenance-plans-and-costs) and [mobile app maintenance](/blog/mobile-app-maintenance-what-to-budget).
Value-based pricing

Value-based pricing sets fees by the value the work creates for the client rather than by your time. If a system saves a company a hundred thousand a year, a fee representing a fraction of that can be both a bargain for the client and highly profitable for you, even if it takes you a fraction of the time. It requires understanding the client’s economics, confidence in your ability to deliver results and credible evidence.

blocks.title: When value-based pricing works
items: You can quantify the client’s gain: revenue, savings, risk reduction
You have relevant case studies and proven outcomes
The buyer is a decision-maker who thinks in business terms, not purchasing hours
You are a specialist rather than a commodity provider
The scope and results can be defined and agreed

blocks.text: It fits automation and integration projects well, where the return can be measured; see [measuring ROI on AI and automation projects](/blog/measure-roi-on-ai-and-automation).
Productised services and packages

Many providers package common services at set prices: a website in a fixed set of pages, an SEO audit, an app discovery sprint, an integration starter package. Productising creates clarity for buyers, shortens sales cycles and lets you refine delivery and become more efficient. It works best for repeatable work and can be combined with optional add-ons and retainers.
Structuring and presenting quotes

items.title: Understand the problem and budget
items.text: Ask about goals, constraints and what success is worth.

items.title: Define the scope clearly
items.text: Deliverables, assumptions and exclusions in plain language.

items.title: Offer options
items.text: Good, better and best packages let clients choose and anchor to value.

items.title: Explain what drives the price
items.text: Transparency builds trust, even if you do not itemise every hour.

items.title: Show the process and timeline
items.text: Milestones, responsibilities and review points.

items.title: Handle changes and extras
items.text: State how additional work will be estimated and approved.

items.title: Set terms
items.text: Payment schedule, validity period and next steps.

items: **Lead with outcomes and value,** not just a list of tasks.
**Include a contingency or ranges** where uncertainty is real.
**Discount scope, not rate:** if the client’s budget is low, offer less, not the same for less.
**Collect deposits** and bill by milestone to protect cash flow.
**Avoid free speculative work;** offer a paid discovery instead.

blocks.text: Protecting yourself from scope creep and bad clients

items: **Written scope and a change-control process:** every addition is estimated and approved.
**Clear acceptance criteria and review periods** so projects can close.
**Payment terms with milestones,** and stop work if invoices go unpaid.
**Limits on revisions** for design or content stages.
**Qualify prospects:** budget, authority, timeline and fit; walk away from poor matches.

blocks.title: Cheap clients are often the most expensive
blocks.text: Clients who negotiate hardest on price tend to demand the most, communicate worst and pay latest. Pricing at a sustainable level filters for better relationships.
Raising your prices

Many providers charge the same rates for years while their skills, reputation and costs grow. Raise prices regularly: for new clients immediately, and for existing ones with notice and justification, perhaps annually or when scope changes. If everyone accepts your quotes without question, you are probably too cheap. Expect some pushback, but also notice that higher prices often improve perceived value and client quality. Support increases with clear results, case studies and improved processes, and offer existing clients a transition period.

blocks.title: Signs it is time to raise prices
items: You win almost every proposal
Your calendar is full and you are turning work down
Your skills and results have clearly improved
Costs have increased and margins have shrunk
You feel resentful about client demands relative to what you earn
Comparable providers charge significantly more

blocks.text: For buyers: reading quotes with this in mind

If you are commissioning software, remember that the cheapest quote may hide missing scope, and the most expensive may include a large risk premium. Compare the scope, assumptions and exclusions, ask how changes are priced and choose the model that matches how clear your requirements are. Our guides on [how to choose a software development company](/blog/how-to-choose-a-software-development-company) and [freelancer vs. agency vs. in-house](/blog/freelancer-vs-agency-vs-in-house) help you evaluate offers.
Common mistakes

items: **Pricing from fear or from competitors’ lowest rates.**
**Fixed prices with vague scope.**
**Forgetting non-billable time and overhead** in rates.
**Free discovery and speculative work.**
**No change process,** absorbing scope creep.
**Never raising prices.**
**Discounting to win work** without reducing scope.

blocks.text: Need a software partner with transparent pricing and clear scope? We offer fixed-price discovery, phased delivery and straightforward support plans so you always know what you are paying for.
blocks.label: Get a clear project quote

faqs.question: Hourly vs fixed price: which is better?
faqs.answer: Fixed price suits well-defined projects and gives cost certainty, while hourly or time and materials suits uncertain or evolving scope. Many providers combine them: fixed-price discovery followed by phased delivery or capped hourly work.

faqs.question: How do I price a retainer?
faqs.answer: Define what is included, such as hours, response times and types of work, estimate the monthly effort, price for the commitment and availability, and set terms for unused hours, reporting and review. Revisit scope and price annually.

faqs.question: How do I raise my rates?
faqs.answer: Raise prices for new clients first, give existing clients notice and justification, support increases with results and improved service, and review prices at least annually.

faqs.question: What is value-based pricing?
faqs.answer: It sets fees according to the value a project creates for the client, such as revenue gained or costs saved, rather than the time spent. It requires understanding the client’s economics and credible evidence of results.

faqs.question: How do I stop scope creep?
faqs.answer: Write a detailed scope with exclusions, define acceptance criteria and use a change-request process where every addition is estimated, approved and priced before work begins.

posts.title: Digital PR and Guest Posting for Tech Companies
posts.description: Digital PR and guest posting for tech companies: find opportunities, pitch editors, write guest articles, earn press coverage and avoid link-spam tactics.
posts.keywords: guest posting for backlinks, does guest posting still work, digital pr for tech companies, how to pitch a guest post, expert commentary journalists, thought leadership, pr for startups
posts.intro: Tech companies often struggle with a particular marketing problem: they build excellent products or services, but few outside their immediate circle know about them. Search visibility depends heavily on authority, and authority comes from being recognised by others: trade publications that quote you, industry blogs that publish your ideas, journalists who cite your data. Digital PR and guest posting are the two most common ways to earn that recognition, and both have been badly damaged by spam. Mass-produced “guest post” services and fake press releases give them a bad name. Done properly, however, they remain some of the most effective routes to credibility, qualified traffic and links that matter. This guide explains how each works, how to find and pitch opportunities, how to write contributions editors actually want, how to build a steady programme and what to avoid.
takeaways: Digital PR earns coverage by giving journalists and editors something genuinely newsworthy: data, expertise, stories and commentary.
Guest posting works when it brings real value to another publication’s audience, not when it is a transaction for a link.
Choose publications for relevance and audience, not just authority metrics; the best placements put you in front of potential customers.
Pitch briefly and specifically, build relationships and respect editorial standards and disclosure rules.
Avoid paid link placements disguised as editorial, mass outreach and low-quality guest post networks.

blocks.text: Digital PR and guest posting: what they are

**Digital PR** is the practice of earning online coverage, mentions and links from news sites, industry publications, blogs and other media by providing material that is worth reporting: original research, expert commentary, newsworthy announcements, compelling stories and useful resources. **Guest posting** (or guest blogging) is writing an article for another website, usually in your field, to share expertise with its audience and build your reputation and, often, earn a contextual link back. Both rest on the same foundation: the people who run publications want content their audiences value, and you can supply it if you have genuine knowledge to share.

blocks.title: Comparing the two approaches
rows: Stories, data, expert quotes and news hooks
You write; editors approve and edit
Credibility, brand awareness and high-authority coverage
Demonstrating expertise and reaching niche audiences
Writing quality content and pitching it
Press mentions, quotes, features and links
Bylined articles, author bios, referral traffic and links

blocks.title: Be clear about your goal
blocks.text: Authority, relationships and customer reach are better goals than “get a link”. Links follow when the work is good, and the best placements bring readers who may become customers.
Has guest posting been ruined by spam?

Google has warned about large-scale guest posting campaigns run primarily to manipulate rankings, with keyword-stuffed anchor text and low-quality articles. Services that sell guest posts on sites that accept payment for any content are a clear example of the problem. But legitimate contribution to relevant publications, with real editorial standards and genuine value for readers, remains valid and valuable. The test is simple: would the article be worth publishing even if there were no link? If so, you are on safe ground; if not, you are producing spam.
Find the right publications
Relevance beats raw authority. A mention in a respected publication read by your target customers is worth more than a link from a large but unrelated site.

blocks.title: Qualities of a good target
items: Its audience overlaps with your potential customers or partners
It publishes high-quality, editorially reviewed content on topics you know
It has real traffic and an engaged readership, not just a high authority score
It does not accept payment for editorial placements or run obvious “write for us” factories
Its guidelines and past contributors suggest genuine standards
It is open to expert contributions or has journalists who cover your field
**Industry trade publications and newsletters** in your sector.
**Business and technology media** that cover your topics.
**Professional associations and communities** with member blogs.
**Podcasts and webinar hosts** whose audience matches yours.
**Local and regional media** for community and business stories.
**Platforms where practitioners publish,** such as professional networks and communities, where authentic expertise is valued.

blocks.text: Build your angles

Editors do not need another generic piece on “five tips for digital transformation”. They need angles that are timely, specific and backed by something others do not have. Start by listing what you uniquely possess.

blocks.title: Sources of newsworthy angles
rows: Anonymised trends from your product or projects, survey results, cost benchmarks
Lessons from real projects, failures and what you would do differently
Reacting quickly to regulatory changes, platform updates or industry events
Case studies with measurable outcomes, with permission
A checklist, calculator or model readers can use

blocks.text: Our guide to [B2B content marketing for tech companies](/blog/b2b-content-marketing-for-tech-companies) explains how to generate and package these assets, and [keyword research](/blog/keyword-research-for-service-businesses) helps identify topics people are actively seeking.
How to pitch a guest post

items.title: Study the publication
items.text: Read recent articles, guidelines and the tone and format they prefer.

items.title: Find the right editor
items.text: Look for the contributor or section editor, and use the channel they specify.

items.title: Propose two or three specific ideas
items.text: Each with a headline, a one-sentence summary and why their readers will care.

items.title: Show your credibility
items.text: A brief line on your experience and a link to relevant work.

items.title: Keep it short
items.text: A few sentences, personal and free of hype.

items.title: Follow up once
items.text: A single polite nudge after a week or two; then move on.

blocks.title: Pitches that work vs. pitches that get deleted

left.title: Works
points: Specific idea tailored to the publication
Clear value for readers, with evidence
Evidence of expertise and writing quality
Respect for guidelines and editorial control

right.title: Gets deleted
points: “I would like to contribute to your site” with no idea
Obvious mass email with the wrong name
Request for a link or payment details up front
Promotional content disguised as an article

blocks.text: Writing the article

items: **Deliver real value:** specific, practical, original insight beats generic advice.
**Follow the publication’s style, length and format** precisely.
**Write for the readers, not for your product:** mention your company lightly, in the author bio or where genuinely relevant.
**Support claims with evidence:** data, examples and credible sources.
**Use clear structure:** an engaging headline, short paragraphs, subheadings, lists and a useful conclusion.
**Offer visuals** such as charts or diagrams if they help.
**Link sparingly and naturally,** to genuinely useful resources, including yours only when they add value.
**Disclose appropriately:** be transparent about affiliations and sponsorships.

blocks.text: Avoid using AI to mass-produce contributed articles. Editors increasingly detect generic, unoriginal text, and the principles in [AI content and SEO: what Google says](/blog/ai-content-and-seo-what-google-says) apply: use tools to assist, but bring real experience and verified facts.
Digital PR in practice
Respond to journalist requests

Journalists often seek expert sources on tight deadlines through request services, social platforms and newsletters. Subscribe, monitor requests relevant to your expertise and respond quickly with a concise, quotable answer and your credentials. Reliability builds relationships.
Publish data and research

A well-designed survey or analysis of your own data can generate coverage for months. Make sure the methodology is sound, the findings are genuinely interesting, the data is presented clearly with a summary and visuals, and the press page offers key stats and quotes. Offer exclusives to relevant journalists when appropriate.
Newsjack responsibly
When news breaks that relates to your expertise, a fast, thoughtful expert comment can earn coverage. Stay relevant and honest, avoid exploiting tragedies and never claim expertise you do not have.
Announcements with substance

Product launches, funding, partnerships and milestones can earn coverage if they matter to the publication’s audience. Press releases alone rarely work; pair them with a story, quotes, assets and direct, personal outreach.
Prepare a press kit

blocks.title: Make it easy for media to work with you
items: A short company description and fact sheet
Biographies and photos of spokespeople
Logos and product images in good resolution
Key data points and the story behind them
A clear media contact with quick response times
Case studies and customer quotes with permission

blocks.text: Relationships over transactions

The most successful PR and guest-posting programmes treat editors and journalists as long-term contacts. Follow their work, share and comment thoughtfully on their articles, send useful tips even when there is nothing in it for you immediately and respond reliably when they ask. Editors remember people who make their jobs easier. This also applies to partners and customers who can amplify your stories: encourage them to share and link naturally.
Disclosure, ethics and what to avoid

items: **Paid placements disguised as editorial:** if you pay, it should be clearly labelled, and links should carry appropriate attributes.
**Guest post factories and link-selling networks,** with low standards and anyone-can-pay policies.
**Exact-match anchor text campaigns** across many posts.
**Fake data, fabricated quotes or exaggerated claims,** which destroy reputation and trust.
**Mass, untargeted pitches,** which waste editors’ time and your credibility.
**Duplicate content:** do not publish the same article on multiple sites.

blocks.text: Our broader guide to [getting backlinks without spamming](/blog/get-backlinks-without-spamming) covers the wider picture of safe link building.
Measuring success

blocks.title: What to track
rows: Relationships built with editors and journalists

blocks.text: Give the programme time. Digital PR and guest posting compound: early placements build credibility that makes later ones easier. Review results quarterly, double down on what works and drop what does not.
Common mistakes

items: **Treating it as link buying.**
**Pitching without reading the publication.**
**Writing promotional content** instead of genuinely helpful articles.
**Chasing authority metrics** instead of audience relevance.
**Giving up** after a few rejections.
**No follow-through:** failing to promote and reference the placements you earn.
**Ignoring disclosure rules.**

blocks.text: Want to be recognised as an authority in your field? We help tech companies build websites, content and credibility that earn coverage, links and qualified traffic.
blocks.label: Strengthen your authority

faqs.question: Does guest posting still work?
faqs.answer: Yes, when done to share real expertise with a relevant audience on a reputable publication. Mass guest posting purely for links is risky and increasingly ineffective.

faqs.question: How do I pitch a guest post?
faqs.answer: Study the publication, address the right editor, propose two or three specific, valuable ideas with a short note on your expertise, keep it brief and follow up once. Follow their guidelines.

faqs.question: What makes a link high quality?
faqs.answer: Relevance, trustworthiness of the site, editorial placement within useful content, natural anchor text and genuine audience. A single relevant editorial link beats many low-quality ones.

faqs.question: What is digital PR?
faqs.answer: Earning online coverage and links from media and publications by offering newsworthy material such as original data, expert commentary and stories, rather than buying placements.

faqs.question: Should I pay for guest posts?
faqs.answer: Paying for placements that pass ranking credit violates search guidelines. Legitimate sponsored content should be clearly labelled and use appropriate link attributes, and should not be relied on for SEO.

posts.title: How to Get Backlinks Without Spamming: A Practical Guide
posts.description: How to get quality backlinks without spam: link-worthy content, digital PR, partnerships, outreach and the tactics to avoid so you stay safe from penalties.
posts.keywords: get backlinks safely, how to build backlinks, white hat link building, do backlinks still matter, how many backlinks do i need, link building for small business, are directory links worth it
posts.intro: Backlinks, links from other websites to yours, remain one of the strongest signals search engines use to judge the authority and relevance of a page. They are also the most abused. Inboxes fill with offers of “500 high-quality links for 50 dollars”, forums are littered with comment spam and businesses get penalised for shortcuts that looked clever. The honest truth is that good link building is slow, requires real effort and works best when it is a by-product of doing something worth linking to. But it is far from mysterious. This guide explains what makes a link valuable, the white-hat strategies that work for small and mid-sized businesses, a practical process for outreach, how to measure results and which tactics to avoid because they invite penalties or simply do not work.
takeaways: Quality, relevance and editorial context matter far more than the number of links.
The most sustainable link building comes from genuinely useful content, original data, real relationships and being visible in your industry.
Effective tactics include digital PR, partnerships, resource pages, broken-link replacement, local and industry directories and thought leadership.
Avoid paid link schemes, link farms, mass guest posting for links and automated spam; they risk penalties and rarely last.
Treat link building as long-term marketing: build assets, build relationships, measure, and be patient.

blocks.text: Do backlinks still matter?

Yes. Search engines began by treating links as votes of confidence, and links remain a major factor in how pages are discovered and ranked, even as other signals have grown in importance. Google has said that links are one of many signals and that its systems have become better at ignoring spam and unnatural patterns. The practical lesson is that earning links from relevant, trustworthy sites helps, while manufactured links add risk and little benefit. Links also drive direct referral traffic and brand visibility, valuable in their own right, including for being cited by AI assistants, as discussed in [generative engine optimization](/blog/generative-engine-optimization-guide).
What makes a link valuable

blocks.title: Qualities of a good backlink
rows: A link from a site in your industry or topic carries more meaning than one from an unrelated site
Links from well-regarded, genuine sites matter more than from unknown or low-quality ones
A link placed naturally within useful content, by an editor’s choice, beats one in a footer, sidebar or paid slot
A link people actually click brings real visitors
Natural, descriptive text helps context; over-optimised exact-match anchors look manipulative
A natural profile includes many different sites and link types

blocks.title: Quantity is a trap
blocks.text: Fifty links from irrelevant directories or networks will not outweigh one genuine link from a respected industry publication, and the fifty may harm you. Focus on earning links that you would be proud to show a customer.
Start with something worth linking to
No outreach technique rescues content nobody wants to cite. Before asking for links, make sure your site has assets that others have a reason to reference.

items: **Original research and data:** surveys, benchmarks or analyses of your own anonymised data are often cited by journalists and bloggers.

**Definitive guides and resources:** comprehensive, well-structured articles that become the reference on a topic, like our [technical SEO checklist](/blog/technical-seo-checklist-for-business-websites).
**Free tools and templates:** calculators, checklists, briefs and templates people share.
**Visual assets:** infographics, diagrams and charts with clear explanations that others can embed with credit.
**Case studies and results:** real outcomes that illustrate trends.
**Strong opinions and expert commentary:** a distinctive, well-argued viewpoint can attract citations.

blocks.text: Our guide to [B2B content marketing](/blog/b2b-content-marketing-for-tech-companies) explains how to produce this kind of material consistently, and the [keyword research guide](/blog/keyword-research-for-service-businesses) shows how to find topics with genuine demand.
White-hat link-building strategies that work
1. Digital PR and being a source

Journalists and editors constantly need expert comment, data and stories. Share original data, offer commentary on news in your field and respond to genuine requests for expertise on platforms and email lists where reporters seek sources. Coverage in news and industry publications brings strong, relevant links and credibility. Pitch only what is relevant, with a clear angle and evidence.
2. Partnerships and relationships

Suppliers, clients, partners, trade associations, chambers of commerce and community organisations often link to businesses they work with, in partner pages, case studies, member directories and event listings. Ask naturally, and offer value in return, such as a testimonial, a case study or a co-created resource.
3. Resource pages and curated lists

Many sites maintain pages listing helpful resources on a topic. If you have a genuinely useful guide or tool, politely suggest it to the maintainer, explaining why it would help their readers. Be specific and brief, and accept a no.
4. Broken-link and unlinked-mention outreach

Find relevant pages with links that no longer work, and if you have a suitable replacement, let the owner know. Similarly, search for mentions of your business or content that do not link to you, and politely ask whether they could add a link. Both are helpful to the site owner, which is why they work.
5. Thought leadership and speaking
Podcasts, webinars, conferences and guest contributions in respected outlets build authority and links when you offer real expertise. Prioritise quality and relevance over volume.
6. Local and industry citations

Reputable local directories, industry associations and chambers of commerce provide useful links, trust signals and local relevance. Choose quality over quantity, and prioritise those real customers might use; see [local SEO for service businesses](/blog/local-seo-checklist-for-service-businesses).
7. Content partnerships and community participation

Contribute genuinely helpful answers in relevant communities, co-author resources with complementary businesses and take part in industry events. Links that result tend to be natural and relevant, and the relationships bring other benefits.
A practical outreach process

items.title: Identify the asset
items.text: Choose a page that deserves links and explain why it is valuable.

items.title: Find relevant targets
items.text: Look for sites that already link to similar resources or cover the topic.

items.title: Research the person
items.text: Find the right contact and understand what they publish and why.

items.title: Write a short, personal message
items.text: Say who you are, why the resource helps their readers and what you suggest. No templates dumped on hundreds of people.

items.title: Follow up once or twice
items.text: A polite reminder after a week or two is fine; then stop.

items.title: Say thanks and build the relationship
items.text: Link-builders who treat contacts well get repeat opportunities.

items.title: Record results
items.text: Track outreach, responses and links earned to learn what works.

left.title: Good outreach
points: Personal, specific and brief
Benefits the recipient’s audience
Targeted at a few relevant sites
Accepts “no” gracefully

right.title: Spammy outreach
points: Generic mass emails
Asks for a link with no reason or value
Offers payment for links or exchanges at scale
Pressure and repeated follow-ups

blocks.text: What to avoid

Google’s spam policies prohibit link schemes designed to manipulate rankings. Practices that violate them can lead to ranking drops or manual actions. Read the current guidelines, and treat the following with extreme caution.

items: **Buying links** or paying for placements that pass ranking credit without proper disclosure and attributes.
**Link exchanges at scale,** “you link to me, I link to you”.
**Private blog networks and link farms:** networks of sites created to link to each other or to yours.
**Mass guest posting** purely for links, especially with exact-match anchors.
**Automated or low-quality directory, forum and blog comment links.**
**Hidden links and manipulative widgets,** such as sponsored widgets stuffed with keyword anchors.
**Expired-domain tricks** and similar shortcuts.
**Over-optimised anchor text** repeated across many links.

blocks.title: Paid and sponsored links need proper attributes
blocks.text: Advertising and sponsorship are legitimate, but links in them should carry the appropriate “sponsored” or “nofollow” attributes so they do not pass ranking credit. Never disguise paid placements as editorial.
AI-generated mass content created to support link building is also risky; see [AI content and SEO: what Google says](/blog/ai-content-and-seo-what-google-says) for the principles.
How many backlinks do you need?

There is no magic number. Compare your link profile with the top-ranking pages for your target queries: how many different sites link to them, and how authoritative are those sites? You need enough relevant, quality links to be competitive, which for local or niche keywords may be few and for highly competitive topics many. Do not forget internal links, which you fully control; see [internal linking strategy](/blog/internal-linking-strategy).
Measuring link-building results

blocks.title: What to track
rows: New referring domains, by relevance and quality
Growth in distinct, valuable sites linking to you
Whether target pages are gaining support
Referral traffic and conversions from links
Rankings and impressions for target queries

blocks.text: Use Google Search Console’s links report and your preferred SEO tool to monitor. Link building shows results over months, not days, so judge progress over a quarter or more.
A starter plan for small businesses

blocks.title: First 90 days
items: Create or improve two or three genuinely link-worthy assets: a definitive guide, a template or tool and a data-based article
Claim and complete relevant local and industry directory profiles and partner listings
Ask satisfied clients and partners for testimonials or case studies that link to you
Identify ten relevant resource pages and publications and send personalised outreach
Offer expert commentary or a data insight to journalists in your niche
Look for unlinked brand mentions and request links
Share your content where your audience gathers, helpfully
Track outcomes and refine your approach

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Chasing quantity** with cheap link packages.
**Skipping the asset:** asking for links to unremarkable pages.
**Mass, generic outreach.**
**Over-optimised anchor text.**
**Ignoring relevance** in favour of authority numbers.
**Expecting quick results,** then giving up or turning to shortcuts.
**No measurement,** repeating what does not work.

blocks.text: Want authority built the right way, with content worth linking to and ethical outreach? We build SEO-ready websites and content strategies that earn links and rankings sustainably.
blocks.label: Build your authority

faqs.question: Do backlinks still matter?
faqs.answer: Yes. Links from relevant, trustworthy sites remain an important signal for discovery and ranking, though quality and relevance matter far more than quantity, and manipulative links carry risk.

faqs.question: How many backlinks do I need?
faqs.answer: There is no fixed number. Compare with pages ranking for your target queries and aim for enough relevant, high-quality referring sites to be competitive. Local and niche terms often need far fewer than highly competitive topics.

faqs.question: Are directory links worth it?
faqs.answer: Reputable local and industry directories can help with trust and relevance, but mass low-quality directories do not. Choose a small number that real customers might use.

faqs.question: Is buying backlinks safe?
faqs.answer: Buying links that pass ranking credit violates search engine guidelines and can lead to penalties. Sponsored placements should be disclosed and use appropriate link attributes, and should not be relied on to rank.

faqs.question: How long does link building take to work?
faqs.answer: Expect months. Earning quality links takes time, and ranking effects lag behind. Focus on assets and relationships, and measure progress over a quarter or more.

posts.description: Google Search Console for beginners: set up, submit sitemaps, read the reports and fix indexing issues like crawled or discovered but not indexed.
posts.keywords: google search console guide, why is my page not indexed, crawled currently not indexed, discovered currently not indexed, submit sitemap search console, search console performance report, fix indexing issues
posts.intro: You publish a page, wait a few days and search for it on Google. Nothing. A week later, still nothing. The page exists, but Google may not have indexed it, or has indexed it and decided not to show it. Google Search Console is the free tool that tells you exactly what Google sees: which of your pages are indexed, which are not and why, which queries bring impressions and clicks, and which technical issues affect your visibility. Many site owners verify their site once and never look again, missing the clearest source of SEO insight available. This beginner’s guide walks through setting up Search Console, submitting your sitemap, reading the key reports, understanding what the indexing statuses mean and fixing the most common problems, with a routine you can follow every month.
takeaways: Search Console shows how Google crawls, indexes and ranks your site, straight from the source.
Verify your site, submit an XML sitemap and use the Pages and URL Inspection tools to diagnose indexing.
“Crawled, currently not indexed” and “Discovered, currently not indexed” usually point to quality, structure or crawl issues rather than a bug.
Fix technical blockers first, then improve content value and internal linking; requesting indexing helps but does not guarantee it.
Review Search Console monthly for performance trends, errors and opportunities.

blocks.text: What Search Console is

Google Search Console is a free service from Google that helps you monitor and troubleshoot your site’s presence in Google Search. Unlike analytics tools, which measure what visitors do once they arrive, Search Console reports on the stage before: whether Google can find your pages, whether it has chosen to index them, which searches show your site and how often people click. It also reports problems such as crawl errors, mobile usability issues, Core Web Vitals and security warnings. It complements [Google Analytics 4](/blog/google-analytics-4-setup-guide) and is essential for the diagnostic work in our [technical SEO checklist](/blog/technical-seo-checklist-for-business-websites).
Step 1: Add and verify your site

Add your site as a property. Google offers two types: a **domain property**, which covers all subdomains and both HTTP and HTTPS versions and is verified through DNS, and a **URL-prefix property**, which covers a specific address and offers several verification methods such as an HTML file, a meta tag or Google Analytics. A domain property is the most complete choice if you can edit your DNS records. Verify with an account that your business controls, and add colleagues and agencies as users rather than sharing logins. Data begins accumulating after verification, so do it early.

blocks.title: Verify every version of your site
blocks.text: If you use a URL-prefix property, verify the exact version you serve, such as the HTTPS version with or without www, and ensure other versions redirect to it. Domain properties avoid this problem.
Step 2: Submit your sitemap

An XML sitemap lists the pages you want search engines to discover, with optional last-modified dates. Submit it under Sitemaps so Google can find new and updated pages efficiently. Make sure it lists only canonical, indexable URLs that return a normal status, not redirects, errors, noindexed pages or duplicates. Most CMS platforms generate a sitemap automatically. A sitemap helps discovery but does not guarantee indexing: it is a suggestion, not a command.

blocks.title: Sitemap checklist
items: Sitemap reachable at a stable URL and referenced in robots.txt
Only canonical, indexable pages included
Updated automatically when content changes
Large sites split into several sitemaps with an index file
Submitted in Search Console, with the report showing success and the discovered URL count
Image or news sitemap entries where relevant, as described in [image SEO](/blog/image-seo-guide)

blocks.text: Step 3: Understand the indexing report

The Pages report (previously called Coverage) shows how many URLs Google knows about, how many are indexed and why others are not. Understanding the statuses saves a lot of worry. Not every non-indexed URL is a problem: duplicate and redirected URLs are supposed to be excluded.

blocks.title: Common statuses and what they mean
rows: Google has the page in its index and it can appear in results
Nothing, unless unexpected pages are indexed
Google fetched the page but chose not to index it for now
Improve content quality and uniqueness, add internal links, check duplication; see below
Google knows the URL but has not crawled it yet
Improve internal linking and site health; avoid low-value URLs; be patient
Google sees duplicates and chose its own canonical
Set a clear canonical tag and reduce duplicate URLs
Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user
Check signals: content similarity, internal links and redirects
Alternate page with proper canonical tag
The page points to another canonical
The page tells Google not to index it
Remove noindex if indexing is wanted
Allow crawling if the page should be indexed
Expected for redirected URLs; update internal links to the final URL
Redirect if there is a replacement; leave true removals as 404 or 410
The page looks empty or like an error but returns a success status
Improve the content or return the correct status code
The server failed when Google requested the page
blocks.caption: Status names and wording evolve; use Search Console’s help text for current definitions.

blocks.text: Diagnosing a page that is not indexed

items.title: Inspect the URL
items.text: Paste it into the search bar at the top of Search Console.

items.title: Read the verdict
items.text: See whether it is on Google, and the reason if not.

items.title: Test the live URL
items.text: Check that it is reachable, not blocked and rendered correctly.

items.title: Check the canonical and rendering
items.text: Confirm Google’s chosen canonical, and view the rendered page and screenshot for missing content.

items.title: Fix issues
items.text: Remove blocks, fix errors and improve content or links.

items.title: Request indexing
items.text: For important pages, request indexing after fixing, understanding that it is a request, not a guarantee.

blocks.text: If the status is “Crawled, currently not indexed”

This means Google looked at the page and decided it was not worth indexing at that time. It is usually a quality or value signal, not a technical failure. Consider whether the page is thin, duplicates other pages, offers nothing beyond what already exists or is buried with no internal links. Strengthen it: add original, genuinely useful content, answer the searcher’s question better than competing pages, improve titles and headings, link to it from relevant, important pages and make sure it is part of your site structure; see [internal linking strategy](/blog/internal-linking-strategy). If it truly has no value, consolidate or remove it.
If the status is “Discovered, currently not indexed”

Google knows the URL, often from your sitemap or a link, but has not crawled it. This often happens on new or large sites where Google is cautious about crawl load, or where it expects low value from the URLs, such as filter combinations and thin pages. Improve site speed and server reliability, prune low-value URLs, strengthen internal links to important pages and ensure the sitemap lists only pages you want. New sites often need weeks to build crawl trust.

blocks.title: Requesting indexing repeatedly does not help
blocks.text: Submitting the same URL again and again will not force indexing and may waste effort. If a page is not indexed after a fix and a request, wait, strengthen the page and links and check again later.
The Performance report

Performance shows how your site appears in Google Search: **impressions** (times your pages were shown), **clicks**, **click-through rate** and **average position**, broken down by query, page, country and device. It is a goldmine for content and SEO decisions.

items: **Find queries with many impressions and few clicks:** improve titles and descriptions, or the page’s match to the query.
**Find pages ranking on the second page** (positions 8 to 20): add depth, examples and internal links to push them up.
**Discover unexpected queries** that suggest new content ideas and keyword opportunities; see [keyword research for service businesses](/blog/keyword-research-for-service-businesses).
**Compare periods** to see the effect of changes and updates.
**Segment by device and country** to spot mobile or regional problems.

blocks.title: Position is an average
blocks.text: Average position blends many queries, locations and result types, so treat it as a trend indicator, not an exact rank.
Other reports worth checking

blocks.title: Search Console reports
rows: Real-user loading, interactivity and stability for URL groups
When pages are flagged poor or need improvement; see [Core Web Vitals explained](/blog/core-web-vitals-explained)
Rich result eligibility and errors for supported markup types
When errors or warnings appear; see [schema markup guide](/blog/schema-markup-guide-for-small-business)
Top linked pages, external linkers and internal link counts
To spot weakly linked important pages
Temporary hiding of URLs and legacy parameter handling

blocks.text: A monthly Search Console routine

blocks.title: What to check each month
items: Performance: trend of clicks and impressions, top queries and pages, big winners and losers
Pages report: new errors, changes in indexed counts, unexpected exclusions
Sitemaps: successful reads and the expected number of discovered URLs
Core Web Vitals and page experience issues
Enhancements and structured data errors
Manual actions and security issues, which should be empty
Links: new important links and weakly linked key pages
Note actions taken and results, so improvements accumulate

blocks.text: During a redesign or migration, Search Console becomes your early-warning system: monitor indexing, errors and traffic closely for weeks, as outlined in the [website redesign SEO checklist](/blog/website-redesign-seo-checklist).
Common indexing blockers to rule out

items: **A leftover noindex tag or robots.txt block** from staging, a classic launch mistake.
**Canonical tags pointing to the wrong URL.**
**Pages only reachable through scripts or forms,** with no crawlable links.
**Content rendered only by JavaScript** that Google fails to process correctly; test with URL Inspection.
**Thin or duplicate content** across many near-identical pages.
**Slow or unreliable servers** that make crawling difficult.
**Orphan pages** with no internal links.
**Redirect chains and loops.**

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Never opening Search Console after verification.**
**Panicking about every excluded URL,** though many are intentional.
**Submitting a sitemap full of noindexed or redirected pages.**
**Requesting indexing instead of fixing the underlying issue.**
**Ignoring performance data** that reveals easy wins.
**Letting the verification lapse** or losing access when staff change.

blocks.text: Pages not showing up in Google? We diagnose indexing and technical SEO issues, fix the blockers and set up monitoring so your content gets found.
blocks.label: Get an indexing audit

faqs.question: Why is my page not indexed?
faqs.answer: Common reasons are noindex or robots.txt blocks, canonical issues, server errors, thin or duplicate content, no internal links or Google simply deciding the page is not valuable enough yet. Use URL Inspection to see the specific reason.

faqs.question: What does “crawled – currently not indexed” mean?
faqs.answer: Google fetched the page but chose not to include it in its index at that time, usually due to quality, duplication or low perceived value. Improve the content, add internal links and make sure it offers something unique.

faqs.question: How do I submit a sitemap?
faqs.answer: In Search Console, open the Sitemaps report, enter your sitemap URL and submit it. Make sure it lists only canonical, indexable pages, and check that Google reads it successfully.

faqs.question: How long does indexing take?
faqs.answer: It can range from hours to weeks depending on site authority, crawl budget and content quality. New sites and low-value pages take longer. Strong internal links and a healthy site help.

faqs.question: Does requesting indexing guarantee my page will be indexed?
faqs.answer: No. It prompts Google to crawl the URL sooner, but indexing depends on quality and technical factors. Fix issues first, then request once rather than repeatedly.
